A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Flow-GRPO and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–D. Retained material can be matched across relocations and renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v4 reports original SD3.5-M fine-tuning results for compositional generation, text rendering and human preference alignment, including baseline comparisons, ablations and generalization tests.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, FLUX.1-Dev fine-tuning, group-size and initial-noise ablations, and twelve-object counting results.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the GRPO objective, ODE-to-SDE conversion, Gaussian policy and KL formulation, and denoising reduction procedure. The additional backbone evaluation and controlled ablations do not revise the proposed algorithm; the DDPO adaptation concerns a comparison method.

E1.justification: Table 4 extends counting extrapolation from five or six objects to twelve objects, retaining training on two to four objects. Existing GenEval, text-rendering, human-preference, DrawBench and T2I-CompBench++ coverage remains. The FLUX experiment uses the existing human-preference task.

E2.justification: Appendix C.1 newly evaluates DDPO, ReFL and Wasserstein-regularized ORW against Flow-GRPO on human preference alignment, substantially broadening the alignment-method comparisons. Earlier SFT, Flow-DPO and Flow-RWR comparisons remain; the existing GenEval comparison moves into the main text.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce FLUX.1-Dev fine-tuning, group-size controls of 6, 12 and 24, shared versus different initial rollout noise, and CLIP/diversity evaluation using 50 DrawBench prompts with 64 images each. These substantially extend the experimental design. Previously stated SD3.5-M splits, rewards and default training/evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 adds a group-size stability ablation, and Appendix C.3 adds an initial-noise exploration ablation, testing distinct questions beyond the existing SDE noise-amplitude analysis. Table 4 extends counting extrapolation to twelve objects. Existing KL, denoising-reduction and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated training-run counts, confidence intervals, standard errors or significance tests. The new group-size and initial-noise experiments vary training conditions; they do not introduce reporting of run-to-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and existing Table 4 entries are unchanged, but substantial results are added. Twelve-object accuracy is 0.02 for SD3.5-M versus 0.12 with Flow-GRPO. Table 6 reports CLIP scores of 28.40 for ORW versus 30.18 for Flow-GRPO. New FLUX results include PickScore 22.62 versus 23.97 and DeQA 4.31 versus 4.24 before and after fine-tuning. New curves also report baseline and ablation findings.

T1.justification: Equations 1–29 and Appendix A's Fokker–Planck, reverse-time SDE and score–velocity derivations are retained. Differences are typesetting, placement and citation numbering; no mathematical definition, assumption or proof is substantively revised.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion narrow the novelty claim from the first integration of online RL into flow matching to the first integration of online policy gradient RL. The headline performance, denoising-reduction and reward-hacking claims retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: v5 attributes small-group instability to inaccurate advantage estimates and explains varied initial noise through increased exploration. Appendix C.1 adds arguments for nondifferentiable VLM rewards, including unevaluated claims about cost-free upgrades. Existing KL interpretations and the limitations paragraph remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds DDPO adaptation details, ReFL gradient timesteps of 30–40, and ORW settings including beta 0.5, alpha 1 and the policy-refresh search. Figure 8 newly explains tuned batch sizes and the prompt-count comparison axis. Core GRPO hyperparameters, hardware and code/model access links remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v5 adds citations for ORW, step-by-step preference optimization, ProRL and AceReason-Nemotron, connecting the latter two to group-size instability. It also expands comparisons with prior alignment approaches and narrows novelty positioning to online policy gradient RL. Most related-work coverage is retained.

P1.justification: The main baseline discussion expands using explanations already present in v4's appendix, and the analysis and appendix organization gain additional subsections. Affiliations, corresponding-author information, acknowledgements and publication text are updated. The core introduction, method exposition and overall narrative remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation expands substantially with group-size, initial-noise and FLUX plots, a DDPO/ReFL comparison panel, and Tables 5–7. Table 4 gains a twelve-object column. The earlier GenEval comparison is resized and moved from appendix Figure 7 to main-text Figure 4, while retained figures are redistributed and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v5 addresses important gaps in v4's empirical support by adding directly relevant DDPO, ReFL and ORW comparisons, quantitative diversity evaluation, and Flow-GRPO training on a second backbone. These strengthen the effectiveness and generality claims, while new ablations clarify stability conditions and the narrower novelty claim improves precision. Run-level uncertainty remains unreported, and the cost-free VLM-upgrade argument is unevaluated, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support.
